replacement: 2. What do ascetic ideals mean? Or, to take one case on which I have often been consulted: what does it mean when an artist like Richard Wagner pays homage to chastity in his old age? In a certain sense he had always done so, of course. But only at the very end did he do it in an ascetic sense. What does this "change of attitude" mean, this radical revolution (for that is what it was)? Wagner swung right round into his own opposite. And what does it mean when an artist swings round into his own opposite? Here, if we are willing to dwell a little on the question, we think at once of the best, strongest, gayest and boldest period that Wagner's life perhaps ever had. It was the time when he was deeply and genuinely absorbed in the idea of "Luther's Wedding." Who knows by what chance we now have the Meistersingers in place of that wedding music? And how much of the one may be an echo of the other? Still, there is no doubt that the theme would have praised chastity. It would certainly have praised sensuality as well; and even so it would have seemed quite in order, and just as Wagnerian. For chastity and sensuality are not necessarily opposed: every good marriage, every authentic, heart-felt love, rises above that opposition. It seems to me that Wagner would have done well to bring this pleasing reality home to his Germans once more, with a bold and graceful "Luther Comedy." There were and are many revilers of sensuality among the Germans, and perhaps Luther's greatest merit is just that he had the courage of his sensuality (it used to be called, prettily enough, "evangelistic freedom "). Even where the opposition between chastity and sensuality really does exist, fortunately it has not needed to be a tragic one for some time now. That should hold for all beings sound in mind and body. They are far from counting their delicate balance between "animal" and "angel" as, on the face of it, one of the principles opposed to existence. The most subtle and brilliant spirits, Goethe and Hafiz for example, have even found in it a further charm of life. Such "conflicts" actually tempt one to live. On the other hand, it is only too clear what happens when these ruined swine are reduced to worshipping chastity (and there are such swine): all they see and worship in it is the opposite of themselves, the opposite of ruined swine. Oh, what tragic grunting and eagerness! Just imagine it. They worship that painful and superfluous contrast which Richard Wagner in his last years undoubtedly wanted to set to music and put on the stage! "For what purpose, forsooth?" we may fairly ask. What did the swine matter to him; what do they matter to us?

replacement: 3. Here we cannot help asking what he really had to do with that manly (ah, so unmanly) country bumpkin, that poor devil and natural, Parsifal, whom he finally made a Catholic by such fraudulent devices. What? Was this Parsifal really meant seriously? One might be tempted to suppose the opposite, even to wish it: that the Wagnerian Parsifal was meant joyously, as the closing play of a trilogy or satyric drama, in which Wagner the tragedian wanted to take his leave of us, of himself, and above all of tragedy, in a fitting and worthy way. He would do it with an excess of the most extreme and flippant parody of the tragic itself, of the ghastly earthly seriousness and earthly woe of old; a parody of the crudest phase in the unnaturalness of the ascetic ideal, a phase long since overcome. As I have said, that would have been quite worthy of a great tragedian. Like every artist, he reaches the supreme peak of his greatness only when he can look down on himself and his art, when he can laugh at himself. Is Wagner's Parsifal his secret laugh of superiority at himself, the triumph of the supreme artistic freedom and artistic transcendency he has at last attained? We might, I repeat, wish it were so; for what can Parsifal amount to, taken seriously? Must we really see in it (in an expression once used against me) the product of an insane hate of knowledge, mind and flesh? A curse on flesh and spirit in one breath of hate? An apostasy and a relapse into the morbid Christian and obscurantist ideals? And, in the end, a self-negation and self-elimination by an artist who until then had put all the strength of his will into the opposite, the highest artistic expression of soul and body? Not only of his art, but of his life too. Remember how enthusiastically Wagner once followed in Feuerbach's footsteps. Feuerbach's motto of "healthy sensuality" rang in Wagner's ears in the thirties and forties of the century, as it did in the ears of many Germans (they called themselves "Young Germans"), like a word of redemption. Did he change his mind on this in the end? For at any rate it seems that in the end he wished to change his teaching on it ... and not only in the Parsifal trumpets on the stage. In the melancholy, cramped and embarrassed lucubrations of his later years, a hundred passages show a secret wish and will: a despondent, uncertain, unavowed will to preach actual retrogression, conversion, Christianity, mediævalism, and to tell his disciples, "All is vanity! Seek salvation elsewhere!" Even the "blood of the Redeemer" is invoked once.

replacement: 6. Schopenhauer took over the Kantian treatment of the æsthetic problem, though he certainly did not look at it through Kantian eyes. Kant believed he was honoring art when he put in the foreground those predicates of the beautiful that make up the honor of knowledge: impersonality and universality. I will not discuss here whether this was a complete mistake. I only want to stress that Kant, like other philosophers, did not approach the æsthetic problem from the experiences of the artist (the creator). He considered art and beauty only from the spectator's standpoint, and so imperceptibly brought the spectator himself into the idea of the "beautiful"! If only the philosophers of the beautiful knew this "spectator" well enough! I mean knew him as a great fact of personality, as a great experience, as a wealth of strong and highly individual events, desires, surprises and raptures in the sphere of beauty! But, as I feared, the opposite was always the case. So from the very beginning our philosophers hand us definitions in which the lack of subtler personal experience squats like a fat worm of crass error. It does so in Kant's famous definition of the beautiful. "That is beautiful," says Kant, "which pleases without interesting." Without interesting! Set this definition beside another, made by a real "spectator" and "artist," Stendhal, who once called the beautiful une promesse de bonheur. Here the one point Kant stresses in the æsthetic position is rejected and struck out: le désintéressement. Who is right, Kant or Stendhal? Our æsthetes never tire of putting into the scales on Kant's side the fact that under the magic of beauty men can look at even naked female statues "without interest." Forsooth, we may laugh a little at their expense. On this ticklish point the experiences of artists are more "interesting," and at any rate Pygmalion was not necessarily an "unæsthetic man." Let us think all the better of the innocence of our æsthetes, mirrored in such arguments. Let us even count it to Kant's honor that he taught with such country-parson naïveté about the peculiar character of the sense of touch! And here we come back to Schopenhauer. He stood much closer to the arts than Kant did, and yet he never got outside the pale of the Kantian definition. How was that? The circumstance is marvelous enough. He reads the phrase "without interest" in the most personal way, out of an experience that in his case must have been part and parcel of his regular routine. On few subjects does Schopenhauer speak with such certainty as on the working of æsthetic contemplation. He says it simply counteracts sexual interest, like lupulin and camphor, and he never tires of praising this escape from the "Life-will" as the great advantage and utility of the æsthetic state. One is in fact tempted to ask whether his basic conception of Will and Idea, the thought that freedom from the "will" is possible only by means of "idea," did not originate in a generalization from this sexual experience. (In every question about the Schopenhauerian philosophy, one should, by the way, keep in mind that it is the conception of a youth of twenty-six. It shares, therefore, not only in what is peculiar to Schopenhauer's life but in what is peculiar to that special period of it.) Let us listen, for instance, to one of the most expressive of the countless passages he wrote in honor of the æsthetic state (World as Will and Idea, i. 231). Let us listen to the tone, the suffering, the happiness, the gratitude, in which such words are spoken: "This is the painless state which Epicurus praised as the highest good and as the state of the gods; we are during that moment freed from the vile pressure of the will, we celebrate the Sabbath of the will's hard labor, the wheel of Ixion stands still." What vehemence of language! What images of anguish and long-drawn revulsion! How nearly pathological is that temporal antithesis between "that moment" and everything else: the "wheel of Ixion," "the hard labor of the will," "the vile pressure of the will." But grant that Schopenhauer was a hundred times right for himself personally. How does that help our insight into the nature of the beautiful? Schopenhauer has described one effect of the beautiful, the calming of the will; but is this effect really normal? As was mentioned, Stendhal, a nature just as sensual but more happily made than Schopenhauer, points to another effect of the "beautiful." "The beautiful promises happiness." For him the essential fact seems to be precisely that beauty excites the "will" (the "interest"). And does Schopenhauer not finally expose himself to the objection that he is quite wrong to regard himself as a Kantian here? That he has altogether failed to understand the Kantian definition of the beautiful in a Kantian sense? That the beautiful pleased him too through an interest, in fact the strongest and most personal interest of all, that of the victim of torture who escapes from his torture? — And to return to our first question, "What does it mean when a philosopher pays homage to ascetic ideals?" Now we have, at any rate, a first hint: he wishes to escape from a torture.

7. Let us beware of pulling dismal faces at the word "torture." In this case there is certainly plenty to deduct and plenty to discount; there is even something to laugh at. For we must not underestimate the fact that Schopenhauer treated sexuality in practice as a personal enemy (including its tool, woman, that "instrumentum diaboli"), and that he needed enemies to keep him in good humor. He loved grim, bitter, blackish-green words. He raged for the sake of raging, out of passion. Without his enemies, without Hegel, woman, sensuality and the whole "will for existence," "keeping on," he would have fallen ill and become a pessimist (for he was not a pessimist, however much he wished to be). Without them Schopenhauer would not have "kept on"; that is a safe wager. He would have run away. But his enemies held him fast, and his enemies always lured him back to existence. His wrath was, as it was for the ancient Cynics, his balm, his recreation, his recompense, his remedium against disgust, his happiness. So much for what is most personal in Schopenhauer's case. On the other hand, much in him is also typical, and only now do we come back to our problem. It is an accepted and indisputable fact that, as long as there have been philosophers in the world, and wherever they have existed (from India to England, to take the opposite poles of philosophic ability), they have felt a real irritation and rancor towards sensuality. Schopenhauer is merely its most eloquent outburst and, for anyone with an ear for it, also the most fascinating and enchanting. Philosophers likewise have a real bias and affection for the whole ascetic ideal; let there be no illusions on this score. Both feelings, as has been said, belong to the type. A philosopher who lacks both is, you may be certain, never anything but a "pseudo." What does this mean? For this state of affairs must first be interpreted: in itself it stands there stupid, for all eternity, like any "Thing-in-itself." Every animal, la bête philosophe included, strives instinctively for an optimum of favorable conditions, in which it can let its whole strength play and attain its maximum feeling of power. With equal instinctiveness, and with a fine perceptive flair superior to any reason, every animal shudders mortally at every kind of disturbance and hindrance that blocks, or could block, its way to that optimum. (I am not talking about his way to happiness, but about his way to power, to action, to the most powerful action, and in fact in many cases his way to unhappiness.) In the same way the philosopher shudders mortally at marriage and at all that could persuade him to it, since marriage is a fatal hindrance on the way to the optimum. Which great philosophers have been married, up to now? Heracleitus, Plato, Descartes, Spinoza, Leibnitz, Kant, Schopenhauer: none was married, and, what is more, one cannot imagine them married. A married philosopher belongs to comedy. That is my rule. As for the exception, Socrates, the malicious Socrates seems to have married ironice, just to prove this very rule. Every philosopher would say what Buddha said when the birth of a son was announced to him: "Râhoula has been born to me, a fetter has been forged for me" (Râhoula means here "a little demon"). An hour of reflection must come to every "free spirit" (granted that an hour of thoughtlessness came first), just as it once came to that same Buddha: "Narrowly cramped," he reflected, "is life in the house; it is a place of uncleanness; freedom is found in leaving the house." Thinking so, he left the house. The ascetic ideal shows so many bridges to independence that the philosopher cannot help exulting and clapping his hands when he hears the story of all those resolute men who one day said nay to all servitude and went into some desert, even granting that they were only strong asses and the absolute opposite of strong minds. What, then, does the ascetic ideal mean in a philosopher? This is my answer, which will have been guessed long ago: when he sees this ideal, the philosopher smiles, because he sees in it an optimum of the conditions for the highest and boldest intellectuality. He does not thereby deny "existence." Rather he affirms his existence, and only his existence, and this perhaps to the point of being not far from the blasphemous wish, pereat mundus, fiat philosophia, fiat philosophus, fiam!
